newsitem.title: CANADA: Congo Minerals unveils ambitious magnesium project.
newsitem.headline: Congo Minerals unveils ambitious magnesium project.

text.p: Congo Minerals Inc unveiled Monday an ambitious plan to build a large magnesium plant in the Republic of Congo (Brazzaville) with production costs lower than its traditionally cheaper light metal rival, aluminum.

"We will be at or below aluminum net cash costs," Congo Minerals' vice president Kim Barkan told reporters after a presentation to industry officials on the sidelines of the World Magnesium Conference here.
Magnesium is currently twice as expensive as aluminum.

Company officials were also flanked by Felix Makosso, minister delegate, responsible for prospecting and mining development in the Republic of Congo, who confirmed that two exploration deals have been signed with Congo Minerals.
Some delegates privately expressed skepticism, particularly those with projects of their own, that such a huge project could come on stream so quickly.

The global magnesium market is 300,000 tonnes a year, and some believe Congo Minerals, if successful, could force a rethink of other projects due on stream over the next five years, such as in Australia and Canada.
Congo Minerals' capital costs would be US$6,500 to $7,500 per tonne of metal in a 50,000 to 100,000 tonnes per year plant.
"We are looking to pour our first metal in the year 2000," Barkan said, though adding later the start-up would be three to five years.
Congo Minerals is a privately held, Toronto based company, whose main shareholders include Yorkton Securities of Vancouver and Rothschild Natural Resources, Barkan said.

The company has been granted two exploration permits, Makola and Youbi, in the Kouilou region which contains an estimated 800 billion tonnes of carnallite ore, the world's biggest deposit, Congo Minerals said.

Initial size of production plant will depend on how many carmakers sign up for metals - magnesium components are used to lighten the vehicle - but minimum production would be 50,000 tonnes annually, Congo Minerals said.
By-products would include potash, table salt, calcium chloride and chlorine.

Mining would be done by in situ leach, with seawater pumped into the ground to bring up a carnallite solution to the surface and processed by electrolysis-based technology originating in the former Soviet Union and adapted by Toronto listed Ashurst Technology Ltd.

Ashurst's Chairman and CEO Benton Wilcoxon said he was also looking to develop new, high performance magnesium alloys which would be attractive to the transportation sector, but are not feasible without a cheap source of magnesium.

Barkan said there was ample amounts of cheap electricity at half a cent per kilowatt hour. Hundreds of megawatts of unused hydroelectric power were fed into the ground at present, and large volumes of natural gas from local oilfields, are flared.
Congo Minerals will spend $10 million on a feasibility study that will take 18 months. "At which point we would be looking for project financing," the company's President, William Burton said.

Following debacles such as Bre-X whose world's "biggest gold find" turned out to be a dud, Barkan estimated that bankers and others in the project would spend a further $40 million to verify the feasibility study.

Congo Minerals officials said they have had preliminary talks with World Bank offshoots who are anxious to stop natural gas flaring, and it was expected that other agencies such as the International Finance Corp would be brought in.
Barkan said it was likely that the Congo government would end up with a 10 to 25 percent stake in the project.
((Huw Jones, New York Commodity Desk 212-859-1646))
